items.title: RustConf 2025 Interview: Ross Townsend, Lawrence Harvey, Divisional Manager - Rust, Rust NYC
items.description:
At RustConf 2025 in Seattle, Xander Cesari sits down on behalf of the Rust Project Content Team with Ross Townsend, Divisional Manager for Rust Engineering at Lawrence Harvey and organizer of Rust NYC, the largest Rust user group on Meetup.

Ross shares a view of the Rust world from both sides: growing grassroots communities in the UK, Australia, and now New York, and building Rust teams for companies across North America. Topics include:

• What makes Rust community events different: welcoming to newcomers at every level, from first-time programmers to pre-1.0 veterans
• Rust NYC and Rust East Coast: an oversubscribed meetup, talks on YouTube, and a 1,700-person Discord
• What companies actually hire for: the traits of good software engineers, plus a path into Rust from any language background
• Open source as a credential: many companies weigh public contributions as heavily as commercial Rust experience, and 60-70% of clients will review your open source code instead of giving a technical test
• The state of the market: an embedded Rust boom driven by medical devices, aerospace, and Industry 4.0, with roughly 13-14x the open roles of six months ago
• Why embedded is the most accepting on-ramp for C and C++ developers, including the motion-sensitive light-up business card that got one candidate a job
• Advice for job seekers: don't give up, use the community, and find the mentor matching happening in Discords across the US

Lawrence Harvey: https://www.lawrenceharvey.com/

items.title: Why AI Agents Need Million-Token Context — Thomas Wolf & Olive Song, MiniMax
items.description:
An intern designed the sparse-attention architecture behind MiniMax M3. That detail comes after Olive Song explains the larger problem the team was trying to solve: short context windows aren’t enough when agents must work across long conversations, tool responses and complex environments. M3 combines a functional one-million-token context window with coding, agentic and multimodal capabilities, allowing it to understand text, images and video within the same model.

Thomas Wolf and Olive Song unpack how MiniMax made that context window efficient, why the company trained M3 as multimodal from its very first step and what happens when that training goes wrong. They also discuss MiniMax’s open research culture, products used by hundreds of millions of people, the role of community feedback in improving open-source models and the internal agent harnesses accelerating the company’s own research. By the end, M3 is no longer just the model being discussed—it is already helping the team build M3.1.

About Thomas Wolf

Thomas Wolf is the co-founder and Chief Science Officer of Hugging Face, the open platform and community for building, sharing and collaborating on machine learning models, datasets and applications.

About Olive Song
Olive Song is the RL Lead at MiniMax, where she works on the research and training behind frontier open-source models including MiniMax M3.

Recorded at the AI Engineer World’s Fair in San Francisco. Stay up to date on our upcoming events and content by joining our newsletter here: https://www.ai.engineer/newsletter

items.title: RustConf 2025 Interview: Tyler Mandry, Rust Language Team Lead, Rust Project
items.description:
At RustConf 2025 in Seattle, the Rust Project Content Team talks with Tyler Mandry, co-lead of the Rust Language Team, about how the lang team works, project goals, interop and Crubit, and a tiling window manager written in Rust.

Tyler shares how a skeptic of "starry-eyed people at Mozilla" spent two weeks hunting a race condition in a senior engineer's C++, read the early Rust blog posts, and decided to invest his career in Rust: implementing generic associated types in Chalk, optimizing coroutines, and joining the lang team. Topics include:

• What a lang team co-lead actually does: an open weekly triage meeting and a weekly design meeting, all on the Rust Zulip
• Project goals as an entry point: propose the work you want to commit to, get team support, and go, like the field projection and reborrowing goals
• How RFCs succeed today: start with a motivating vision, then experiment in the compiler before writing everything down
• One-way and two-way doors, preserving optionality, and why nobody has to be the person in the basement with a cork board and a million strings
• Status-quo bias and learned helplessness: why Tyler thinks people are too scared to change Rust, and why small deltas should still add up to a cohesive vision
• Interop as what lets Rust take over the world: CXX today, Crubit's third wave of more integrated Rust-C++ interop tomorrow
• Glide: his third attempt at a macOS tiling window manager (after Lua and Swift), built on objc2 and an actor architecture
• Where Rust isn't the best fit: shell scripts, front ends, and knowing when to take the better-lit path

Tyler's RustConf 2025 talk with Taylor Cramer on Rust-C++ interop and Crubit:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z5M4NIWoMJQ

items.title: RustConf 2025 Interview: Pete LeVasseur, Lead, Safety-Critical Rust Consortium
items.description:
At RustConf 2025 in Seattle, Tyler Mandry, co-lead of the Rust Language Team, sits down on behalf of the Rust Project Content Team with Pete LeVasseur, lead of the Safety-Critical Rust Consortium, to ask: what does safety critical actually mean, and where does Rust fit?

Pete shares the path from mainframe assembly ambitions to a decade in automated driving and ADAS in Metro Detroit, a six-month Haskell side quest, and finding in Rust the answer to the C and C++ defects he kept catching (and worrying about missing) in code review. Topics include:

• What makes software safety critical: potential impact on human life, health, environment, or property, and the regulations that follow from that
• ISO 26262 and the ASIL levels from QM through D, illustrated from infotainment to camera perception to the brake controller
• Safety-qualified toolchains, coding guidelines, and why "subset the language" is literally written into the standard
• Macros in safety critical: escaping the reputation of C macros, and guidelines that offer alternatives instead of just prohibitions
• Where C still wins: exotic ultra-cheap microcontrollers with strange integer widths, glued into cases
• The FLS, "the specification formerly known as the Ferrocene Language Specification": moving to updates every stable release, and what a fuller specification could unlock for multiple compiler implementations like gccrs
• MISRA's recategorization finding that roughly half of MISRA C is simply disapplied by Rust's language guarantees
• MC/DC coverage and the open design questions of applying it to constructs like match
• The consortium today: around 150 members from Infineon to Airbus to Volvo Cars, three subcommittees (Coding Guidelines, Liaison, Tooling), and how joining is as simple as a GitHub issue

Links mentioned:

Safety-Critical Rust Consortium: https://github.com/rustfoundation/safety-critical-rust-consortium
Safety-Critical Rust Coding Guidelines: https://github.com/rustfoundation/safety-critic
